title: Architecture & Standards: API, Coding, Infra, Model-Serving, Observability, Performance
author: Aisha Khan
body:
Purpose
-------
This page consolidates Redwood Inference's cross-cutting architecture and standards for: API design, coding practices, infrastructure, model-serving, observability, and performance. The goal is a single, actionable reference teams can follow to ensure consistent, reliable, and measurable service delivery across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments.

Scope
-----
Applies to: all backend services, public and internal APIs, inference runtime components, control plane services, and operational tooling used in production and staging environments. Does not replace team-level design docs or ADRs — it supplements them with company-wide constraints and conventions.

Principles
----------
- Developer ergonomics first: standard patterns and examples that reduce onboarding time.
- Production safety: defaults favor reliable, observable, and secure behavior.
- Measurable SLOs and clear ownership for every service.
- Backwards-compatible evolution: versioning and deprecation policies required for public APIs and model contracts.

1) API Standards
----------------
Overview: APIs are the primary contract for customers and internal services. Follow RESTful and OpenAPI-first design for public endpoints; internal RPC is permitted for high-performance paths when justified and documented.

Key requirements:
- Versioning: always include major version in the URL, e.g., /v1/models/:id/predict. Increment major version for incompatible changes.
- OpenAPI: every public or shared API must publish an OpenAPI 3.0 spec stored in the api-specs repo and linked from the service README.
- Authentication: use mTLS for service-to-service within control plane networks, and OAuth2 (JWT Bearer) for external customers. Tokens must be validated for scope and expiry.
- Pagination: cursor-based pagination for list resources; support page_size (max 1000) with sensible defaults (page_size=100).
- Rate limiting: per-route rate limits defined in route config; include Retry-After header for 429 responses.
- Idempotency: write endpoints that may be retried (e.g., start-job) must accept Idempotency-Key header and return 409 for conflicting keys.
- Error model: standard error envelope: {"code": string, "message": string, "details": optional list}. Map HTTP codes to these high-level classes: 4xx (client), 429 (throttling), 5xx (server).
- Timeouts: default request timeout for public endpoints is 30s, configurable per-route. Long-running jobs must be exposed as asynchronous operations.

Example: OpenAPI snippet (required for all public endpoints)
--------------------------------------------------------
openapi: 3.0.3
info:
  title: Infer Gateway API
  version: 1.0.0
paths:
  /v1/models/{model_id}/generate:
    post:
      summary: Generate text from a model
      parameters:
        - in: path
          name: model_id
          schema:
            type: string
      requestBody:
        required: true
        content:
          application/json:
            schema:
              $ref: '#/components/schemas/GenerateRequest'
      responses:
        '200':
          description: successful response
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                $ref: '#/components/schemas/GenerateResponse'

2) Coding Standards
--------------------
Overview: aim for readability, testability, and predictable runtime characteristics. Languages and frameworks should be chosen per-service domain; however, standards below apply across all codebases.

Conventions:
- Languages: Python (3.10+) for orchestration/control-plane services, Go (1.20+) for high-throughput network services, Rust allowed for new runtime components when performance-critical.
- Formatting: enforce code style via pre-commit + CI (black/isort/ruff for Python, gofmt/golangci-lint for Go, rustfmt for Rust).
- Type safety: prefer typed interfaces — use mypy/pyright for Python; surface types in public SDKs.
- Unit and integration tests: target >= 70% coverage for core service logic; each PR must include tests for new behavior.
- Dependency management: pin direct dependencies; use automated dependency scanning and regular upgrade cadence (quarterly).
- Secure coding: validate all external inputs, sanitize logs to avoid PII, and rotate secrets using KMS integrations.
- Commit messages: follow Conventional Commits format.

3) Infra Standards
------------------
Naming and ownership:
- Service naming: <team>-<service>-<environment> (examples: infer-gateway-prod, model-onboard-staging).
- Tags: all cloud resources must include tags: owner, team, project, environment, cost-center.
- IaC: Terraform is the canonical IaC tool. Modules live in infra/modules. All PRs changing infra must go through the infra CI and a manual approval if they touch network or IAM.

Network and security:
- VPCs and subnets: dedicated VPC per environment with explicit peering rules for private deployments.
- Security groups: default-deny, least-privilege.
- KMS: customer keys must use dedicated KMS resources and follow the Private deployment key management guide.

Capacity, cost, and autoscaling:
- GPU pools: capacity claims for Dedicated must be declared in the capacity catalog; autoscaling policies should set target utilization 65–75% for steady-state workloads.
- Cost allocation: use resource-level tags and enforce monthly cost reports per team.

4) Model-Serving Standards
--------------------------
Scope: runtime, model packaging, quantization profiles, kernel selection, caching behavior, and deployment choreography.

Model packaging and metadata:
- Model manifest (YAML) required for every model version with fields: model_id, version, architecture, quantization_profile, supported_max_seq_len, recommended_batch_size, owner_team, performance_profile_id. Example fields must be included in the model registry.
- Model versioning: semantic-style versions (major.minor.patch) where major indicates incompatible interface changes (tokenizer changes, output schema).

Runtime and performance:
- Quantization: each model must declare verified quantization profiles (fp16, int8, nf4) and a perf/quality tradeoff note.
- Kernel selection: runtime must pick kernels based on architecture and HW capability; kernel fallback must be logged with reason.
- KV caching: prefix cache enabled by default for chat-style workloads; cache TTL and size quotas set per-customer route.
- Routing policy: requests may be routed by latency or cost; route policy config must declare fallback model variants.

SLOs and regression policy:
- Per-model SLOs: default latency SLO (p50/p95/p99) and availability: p50 < 30ms per-token, p95 < 120ms per-token, p99 < 500ms per-token under steady-state. Availability target: 99.95% for hosted control plane routes.
- Quality guardrails: each new model/version must pass a regression test suite (prompt set) with defined thresholds for accuracy/fluency for the workload. Failures trigger blocking in the rollout pipeline.

5) Observability Standards
-------------------------
Metrics:
- Metric prefixes: service.* for business metrics; infra.* for infra-level; runtime.* for inference internals (tokens_generated_total, kv_cache_hit_ratio, model_latency_seconds).
- Required metrics: request_count, request_latency (p50/p95/p99), error_count (4xx, 5xx), tokens_generated_total, kv_cache_hit_ratio, model_fallback_count.
- Labels: include service, version, model_id, region, route in metric labels.

Tracing and Logs:
- Traces: instrument critical request paths end-to-end with trace IDs (W3C traceparent). Maximum trace sampling for debug environments, 10% default for production, 100% sample for error signals.
- Logs: structured JSON logs, 3 retention tiers (7d hot, 30d warm, 365d cold) with retention policy configurable per tenant. Redact PII and sensitive headers prior to emission.

Dashboards and Alerts:
- Dashboards: every service must publish a Service Overview dashboard (latency, errors, throughput, top-5 slow endpoints, model-specific KPIs).
- Alerts: tie alerts to actionable runbooks. Example thresholds:
  - SLO burn rate > 2 for 30 minutes -> P1 alert.
  - p95 latency > 2x baseline for 15 minutes -> P2 alert.
  - error_rate > 0.5% sustained for 10 minutes -> P2 alert.

6) Performance Standards and Testing
-----------------------------------
Benchmarks and objectives:
- Latency targets (service-level): p50 < 50ms, p95 < 200ms for control plane calls; inference token latency as noted in Model-Serving Standards.
- Throughput: define per-service throughput targets in README and capacity catalog.

Testing and validation:
- Load testing: each release that affects runtime or network path must include a load test run in the performance lab. Use the benchmark harness in eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite.
- Chaos testing: periodic game-days and targeted chaos tests for critical dependencies (DB, cache, model store) at least quarterly.
- Regression detection: automated perf-regression checks in CI; regressions > 10% in p95 latency block merges for runtime and serving components.

7) Decision Records (ADRs) and Governance
----------------------------------------
- ADRs are the canonical record for architecture decisions. Place ADRs in the repo: docs/adrs/<YYYYMMDD>-<short-title>.md and link from service READMEs.
- Required fields for ADR: title, status, context, decision, consequences, owner, date.
- Review cadence: architecture council meets monthly to review new ADRs; any ADR that increases cost or changes security posture requires architecture council approval.

Example recent ADRs:
- 2026-02-14: Use Go for high-throughput network path services (owner: Marcus Lee).
- 2026-03-04: Enforce OpenAPI-first for external APIs (owner: Priya Desai).
- 2026-06-01: Standardize model manifest schema and adopt semantic model versioning (owner: Diego Alvarez).

8) Rollout and Release Guidance
-------------------------------
Minimum checklist for production rollout:
1. OpenAPI spec published and validated.
2. Model manifest present and registered.
3. Automated regression tests (functional + perf) passing.
4. Service overview dashboard deployed.
5. Runbook and oncall owner assigned.
6. Gradual rollout policy configured (10% -> 50% -> 100%) with automatic rollback on defined signals (error_rate, SLO burn).

9) Ownership and Contacts
------------------------
- Architecture council (contact: architecture@redwood.example.com).
- Default owners for this document: Aisha Khan (author), engineering-standards@redwood.example.com.

Appendix: Quick config tables
---------------------------
Service tags required:
| tag_key      | description                    | example              |
|--------------|--------------------------------|----------------------|
| owner        | primary owner (person/team)    | eng-infra            |
| team         | owning team                    | serving-runtime      |
| project      | project identifier             | infer-platform       |
| environment  | prod/staging/dev               | prod                 |
| cost-center  | chargeback identifier          | cc-310               |

Model manifest required fields (summary):
- model_id
- version
- architecture
- quantization_profile
- supported_max_seq_len
- recommended_batch_size
- performance_profile_id
- owner_team

Change log
----------
- 2026-03-04: Initial consolidation (Aisha Khan).
- 2026-06-10: Added KV cache and routing policy requirements (Diego Alvarez).
- 2026-12-05: Clarified SLO numbers and OpenAPI enforcement (Marcus Lee).

If you have questions or need an exception, open an architecture request via the Architecture Council board and include owner, rationale, and proposed mitigations.
